title: Golden datasets
summary: A golden dataset is a versioned set of inputs with expected behaviour (reference answers, relevant document ids, tool sequences or a rubric) that every candidate is scored against. Its value comes from who labelled it, how each row was made and whether it stays held out.
useIf: You need a repeatable yardstick to compare versions of a prompt, retriever, model or agent.
avoidIf: You treat a public benchmark as your yardstick, or you let the team tune on the same rows it reports on.

explain.md: A **golden set** is the fixed set of cases you trust. Each row holds an input and a way to judge the result: a reference answer, relevant document ids for retrieval, an expected tool sequence, or a rubric. Four sources feed it, and each has a different failure profile.

explain.md: Start small. Anthropic advises that 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start, because early changes have large effects; mature agents need larger and harder sets to detect small ones [[r17]]. Record **how each row was made** (hand, trace, synthetic) and the **dataset version**. LangSmith creates dataset versions automatically when examples change, supports tags so CI can target one, and uses splits to group examples [[r29]].

explain.md: **Contamination** has two meanings. Models can have seen a public benchmark in training. GAIA withholds the answers to 300 of its 466 questions to power a leaderboard [[r33]], and SWE-bench Verified is a 500-sample human-validated subset of a 2,294-problem set [[r34]]. A survey describes benchmark data contamination as a significant issue that makes evaluation results unreliable [[tr7]]. Separately, your team can overfit its own set. Keep a **held-out** slice that no one tunes against and report on it.

explain.title: Secondary source, checked 2026-10-13
explain.md: A secondary write-up reports that OpenAI stopped evaluating on SWE-bench Verified in February 2026 after saturation and flawed tests [[r48]]. The primary page could not be fetched, so treat the numbers as unconfirmed.

pitfalls.symptom: Dev scores climb but production quality is flat
pitfalls.cause: The team tuned prompts against the same rows it reports on
pitfalls.fix: Keep a held-out split, tune on dev only and refresh the held-out slice on a schedule

pitfalls.symptom: Two experts disagree on half the labels
pitfalls.cause: The guideline is ambiguous and no one owns it
pitfalls.fix: Name one accountable expert, write the rubric, and keep disagreements as tagged ambiguous cases

pitfalls.symptom: The set stops matching real queries
pitfalls.fix: Add triaged failing traces on a cadence and drop retired cases with a version bump

scenarios.title: Pre-launch, two expert hours a week
scenarios.situation: A team is building an internal policy assistant. There are no traces, a corpus of 3,000 documents, and one policy expert with two hours a week.
unknowns: Which questions caused trouble in manual trials?
Is the expert willing to own the guideline?
scenarios.question: How do you build the first golden set?

options.name: 30 expert-reviewed cases from observed failures, plus reviewed synthetic cases, with a held-out slice
options.why: It uses scarce expert time on the hardest rows and borrows synthetic breadth, with provenance tags so you can tell them apart.
options.tradeoff: Coverage is a guess until traces arrive.

options.name: 2,000 synthetic cases with no review
options.why: Unreviewed rows can be easy or wrong, so scores mean little.
options.tradeoff: Synthetic is fine at volume once a reviewed sample shows the generator is sound.

options.name: Adopt a public question-answering benchmark
options.tradeoff: It says little about your policies and may be leaked or saturated.

flips.if: Launch slips and a pilot produces traces
flips.then: Mine the pilot traces for new rows.
Double-label a sample and measure agreement.

scenarios.takeaway: Few expert rows beat many unreviewed ones.

scenarios.title: Live product, large trace volume, privacy rules
scenarios.situation: A customer assistant has run for six months with a million logged conversations. Content includes personal data, and the policy allows reuse only after redaction.
constraints: PII must be removed before reuse
unknowns: Which segments matter most to the business?
scenarios.question: How do you refresh the golden set?

options.name: Stratified sample of redacted traces, expert-labelled, versioned monthly, with a frozen held-out core
options.why: Stratifying covers rare segments, redaction satisfies policy, and the frozen core keeps a stable baseline across months.
options.tradeoff: Ongoing labelling effort and redaction review.

options.name: Use the most frequent queries only
options.why: It over-represents easy repeated queries and hides tail failures.
options.tradeoff: Right for a latency or caching study where frequency is what matters.

options.name: Keep the original set unchanged
options.tradeoff: It drifts away from real users and gives false comfort.

flips.then: Write synthetic look-alike cases from failure clusters instead of reusing text.

flips.if: The product shifts to a new domain
flips.then: Start a new set and retire the old one.

scenarios.takeaway: Stratify, redact, version and keep a frozen core.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a held-out slice?
options: To report results on rows nobody tuned against
quiz.explain: A held-out slice detects overfitting to your own set. Size, storage and speed are unrelated.

quiz.q: GAIA has 466 questions and withholds answers to 300 for its leaderboard. What percentage of questions is public developer data?
Which practices keep a golden set trustworthy over time? Select all that apply.
options: Tag each row as hand, trace or synthetic
Version the dataset when examples change
Keep a held-out slice out of tuning
quiz.explain: Provenance, versioning and a held-out slice protect meaning. Adding every trace without triage fills the set with noise and PII.

flashcards.front: How large should a first golden set be?
flashcards.back: 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a strong start. Large early effects need small samples. Grow it as changes get subtler.
Models may have seen a public benchmark in training, and your team may overfit its own set. Withhold answers or keep a held-out slice to control both.

flashcards.front: What should each golden row record?
flashcards.back: Input, reference or rubric, source (hand, trace, synthetic), tags, split and dataset version.
